Some mornings the mind feels less like a machine and more like weather: pressure dropping here, one stray cloud, sun breaking through at an angle nobody predicted. I don’t always trust its forecast. Anxiety says rain in an hour; the sky, indifferent and blue, declines. Still, the forecast is useful as data—not the world, just one instrument drifting across a field.

Lately I’ve been noticing how much of my life happens in the minute before the answer. Before speaking, before deciding, before opening the email or the drawer or the hand. That suspended second is tiny and crowded. It contains habit, fear, memory, courtesy, appetite, maybe love. If I rush it, I inherit my first impulse. If I linger, even briefly, I get a little room to choose.

Choice doesn’t always make us heroic. Sometimes it means choosing gently: hot tea instead of more caffeine, a walk instead of a refresh, a question instead of a verdict. The point isn’t optimization; it’s contact—with sensation, with other people, with the ordinary fact that this is happening now, briefly.

There is mercy in not knowing how a day will unfold. A blank page, an unopened map, a city at dusk, a conversation unfinished—these are thresholds, not problems. Met with attention rather than grasping, they return something strange: not certainty, exactly, but presence, which is sturdier.

So today: less judge, more witness. Notice the weather. Let the sky be the sky. Answer the world in a voice that has listened first.
